In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the defect(s) causing extreme insulin resistance in the patient groups studied are not located in the insulin receptor or its immediate downstream effector mechanisms, but rather are located further downstream in the signal transduction pathway of insulin action.
insulin-stimulated receptor autophosphorylation is normal in cultured Epstein Barr virus transformed lymphocytes derived from patients with insulin-resistant syndromes.

insulin receptor phosphorylase in cultured lymphocytes is not abnormal in extreme insulin resistant subjects, and therefore does not seem to be a primary abnormality in the etiology of extreme insulin resistance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insulin receptor phosphorylations appear normal in cultured lymphocytes from patients with extreme resistance to insulin action.

insulin-stimulated receptor kinase activity is normal in cultured lymphocytes from patients with extreme forms of insulin resistance, including the rare patients with extreme resistance to insulin's effects on glucose metabolism.

insulin-stimulated receptor autophosphorylation is a normal response in B-lymphoblastoid cell lines derived from normal and insulin-resistant subjects, and the magnitude of the response to insulin is not related to the degree of insulin resistance in the patient from whom the cell lines were derived.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, at least at the level of insulin receptor phosphorylation, the insulin resistance seen in these patients is not caused by a defect in the insulin receptor itself.

the insulin-stimulated phosphorylative response of the insulin receptor appears to be normal in cultured lymphocytes derived from patients with clinical syndrons of extreme insulin resistance, and that the defect in insulin action is probably distal to the insulin receptor.
insulin-stimulated phosphorylations of the insulin receptor appear normal in lymphocytes from patients with extreme resistance to insulin action.
